doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

chapter: Studio philosophy: making the artist comfortable
title: Setting up a comfortable studio for the artist
summary: Hank describes arranging the room so the band wraps around the artist, with water, clean cups and a comfortable stool, rather than isolating players in booths.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: The thing that worked better was, having worked with Lou Adler and I worked with Lou a lot, and he was such a great producer. You know he did the Mamas & Papas and all that stuff. I started working with Lou and Carole King and my thing has always been to make sure that the artists were comfortable. I know there are a lot of engineers that get into arguments about earphones, before they even started a date. And stuff like that. My thing was always to try to make it as comfortable as possible. I would keep the lights in the control room down. They didn’t need to see us. You know? We needed to see them. And it helped because then the artists were not tied down into looking into the booth to see what the producer was doing and what the engineers were doing. If I kept the lights down and the lights in the studio up and I tried to make it as comfortable as possible, I would set up dates where if it was a rhythm section and an artist singing I would try to wrap the band around the artist. Even if the artist was in a booth I always tried to set it up so that everybody could see each other and then it was much more of a feeling. A lot of engineers would put the drums in a drum booth, the guitar into this booth. I never felt that really worked. Putting the artist maybe in a vocal booth was okay because you might want to do the vocals over again or the artist felt it was more comfortable, and sometimes we just did it and it worked fine. But some artists, they wanted to come back in again and do the vocals. So you had to work with that situation, make them comfortable was always the object of the whole thing. I saw dates the guys would set up and they’d put the artist right in the middle of the room facing the control room and everybody’s looking at the artist and they’re getting a little bit uncomfortable. I always tried to make it really comfortable for an artist and it was a thing that a lot of guys didn’t think about. For me, I would set up a vocal booth and I’d make sure there was water there, I’d make sure there were clean cups, I made sure if there was a chair or stool that the artist was sitting on was comfortable. I tried to make it as comfortable as possible out in the room. I remember, I saw guys with artists, even if they were overdubbing they’d put them in a booth with a microphone in there and then like they felt they were locked in. Some people just worked fine, other people felt really constricted by working that way.
Did you work with producers that tended to over-hype the artist, like give them pep talks: “You’re going to be great, this is going to be terrific”?
